conclusion.justification: The report finds that opening a bedroom window is supported by evidence to improve sleep quality by reducing CO2 levels, though opening a door alone does not yield the same benefits. Because it generally supports the window aspect of the claim while noting context-dependent limitations (such as noise, pollution, and temperature), it is labeled as leans_endorse.
conclusion.label: leans_endorse

report:
The claim that opening a bedroom window improves sleep quality is supported by evidence, but opening a door alone does not appear to have the same effect.

A 2022 field intervention study found that sleeping with an open window objectively and subjectively improved sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance by reducing bedroom carbon dioxide (CO2) concentrations. In contrast, opening a bedroom door reduced CO2 levels but did not provide the same sleep benefits. A follow-up study confirmed that opening a window is a more effective way to improve bedroom air quality and sleep than opening an internal door.

The mechanism behind this improvement is better indoor air quality (IAQ). Research indicates that if ventilation keeps CO2 levels below 750 ppm, the air quality is good enough that it does not negatively affect sleep. 

However, the benefits of opening a window are context-dependent. Experts note that for people in areas with clean outdoor air, minimal allergens, and low noise, open windows may improve sleep quality and overall health. Conversely, if the outdoor environment is noisy, polluted, or has extreme temperatures, opening a window could disrupt sleep rather than enhance it.
